overall_summary: Analysis of deduplicated observations shows exceptional traction for space and extreme planetary scenarios—specifically 'What If' hypothetical formats featuring rare cosmic bodies, extreme physics, and high-value or exotic materials (diamonds, dark planets, unusual rain types). Engagement metrics (likes-per-view) spike on high-concept cosmic what-if questions and visual contrasts, while standard biological or psychological facts show lower relative velocity in this dataset.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (IYuce8vaU3Y) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (8KEl0_pJ_68) pull over 900-1000+ views rapidly with high like conversion (e.g., 38 likes on ~1k views).
winning_patterns.action: Produce more hypothetical planetary survival and extreme physics scenarios using visually striking environments.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing bizarre planetary conditions—such as 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' (v1rrcZLdp4U) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (QXuqYERlqSo)—achieve strong view velocity and audience resonance.
winning_patterns.action: Continue targeting lesser-known exoplanets with extreme, counter-intuitive physical phenomena.

weak_patterns.evidence: Videos focusing on internal psychological tricks or generic brain functions (e.g., 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories', 'Your Brain Is Hiding This From You') stagnate with low view counts (<60 views) and zero engagement.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize standalone psychological facts unless paired with a high-stakes narrative or extreme scenario.

weak_patterns.evidence: Basic animal facts without existential or cosmic framing (e.g., standard octopus or jellyfish facts) exhibit lower velocity compared to space content.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot animal concepts into cinematic survival or extreme evolutionary anomalies rather than simple listicle facts.
